newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-ADVERTISING, SATELLITE UPS M-NET .
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-ADVERTISING, SATELLITE UPS M-NET .

text.p: Bumper advertising revenues and subscription income from its new satellite television service is expected to back a leap in year results at South African pay-television firm M-Net, analysts said on Thursday.

Electronic Media Network Ltd, which trades under the name M-Net, is seen reaping benefits from advertisers' switch from state broadcaster SABC after it suffered a disastrous channel relaunch and continued management and financial troubles.
"Advertising revenue growth has been good. Because the SABC was in so much trouble, M-Net was able to revise up its rates," said John Biccard, an analyst at HSBC Simpson McKie.

The Economist Intelligence Unit, a grouping which tracks economic trends worldwide, said in April that M-Net secured advertising growth of 18.2 percent in calender 1996. The SABC managed only 2.2 percent, it said.

Analysts polled by Reuters forecast M-Net's headline earnings per share for the year to March 31 rising to between 18.0 and 20.9 cents with consensus at 19.6 cents -- a jump of 25 percent over last year's 15.7 cents.
The firm is due to report results from Tuesday next week.
M-Net earlier this year declared an annual dividend of 11.0 cents compared with 10.0 cents in 1995/1996.

Although growth in subscriber revenues at M-Net, which last year added its one millionth subscriber, was slowing it was gaining from some viewers' switch to its more expensive digital satellite television channels, DStv, launched late in 1995.
"What we have seen over the past few months is a switch from analogue to DStv. M-Net can earn more from this subscriber base and that would drive revenues," another analyst said.
Another boon was that associate MIH Holdings Ltd , which manages M-Net's subscriptions in South Africa, the rest of Africa and Europe, had shouldered the start-up costs of the satellite venture.
MIH is due to report results at the same time as M-Net.
Some analysts said that M-Net may in future lose some advertisers as it had become very expensive.
"Quite a few advertisers are looking at SABC again as it is dirt cheap compared to M-Net," one said.
The SABC, which last year posted a 60 million rand loss in the year to end-September, was recently granted an additional 177 million rand to fulfill its role as public broadcaster.
Under severe financial pressure and suffering from a spate of senior resignations, the SABC also announced in March that it would have to cut up to 1,400 jobs.
